title: Autoscaling Economics
summary: The cost side of scaling decisions — every autoscaling policy prices a trade-off between idle headroom and the risk of not having capacity when it's needed.

slides.markdown:
Autoscaling isn't just a mechanic — it's an economic decision every time it fires. Every scale-up trades money for safety margin; every scale-down trades margin for savings. Get the timing or thresholds wrong and you either pay for headroom nobody used, or save money right up until a spike takes the service down.

- The knob you're really tuning is **risk tolerance**, priced in dollars per hour.
- The mechanics (HPA, Cluster Autoscaler) live elsewhere — this is what the decisions cost.

Every autoscaling policy balances two costs that never show up on the same line item. **Headroom cost** is what you pay for capacity sitting idle, ready for a spike that may not come. **Underprovisioning risk** is what you pay in failed requests or breached SLOs when a spike arrives before enough capacity does.

There's no zero-cost setting — tune purely for savings and a spike will eventually outrun you; tune purely for safety and you'll carry expensive idle capacity most of the day. The right setting depends on how expensive an outage is versus how expensive standing headroom is.

| | Reactive | Predictive |
|---|---|---|
| Trigger | Current metric crosses a threshold | Forecast of expected future load |
| Lag | Scales up *after* load already arrived | Can scale up *before* load arrives |
| Data needed | Live metrics only | Historical patterns, seasonality |
| Risk | Slow to react to sudden spikes | A wrong forecast over- or under-provisions |

**How to decide:** reactive is simpler and fine for gradual load changes; predictive earns its complexity for known, recurring spikes — daily peak hour, a seasonal sale — where waiting for a threshold breach is already too late.

Scale-to-zero shuts a workload down entirely when there's no traffic, paying nothing while idle. It's a real saving for workloads with long idle stretches — an internal tool used a few times a day, a batch job that only runs nightly.

The trade-off is the **cold start** on the way back up: the first request after idle waits for a fresh instance to boot, sometimes seconds. For a workload with steady baseline traffic, scale-to-zero just means paying that cold-start latency on nearly every request, since it never actually reaches zero — worse for users, with no real savings.

Spot/preemptible instances are cheap because the provider can reclaim them with little notice — surviving on spot means designing for interruption, not avoiding it. The core strategy is **diversification**: spreading a fleet across several instance types and availability zones, so a reclamation wave in one pool doesn't take out the whole fleet at once.

Pair this with fast, cheap instance replacement and a fallback slice of on-demand capacity for the portion of load that truly can't tolerate interruption.

slides.subTitle: On-demand baseline plus spot burst
slides.markdown:
A batch-processing service needs 20 workers online at all times, bursting to 100 during nightly peaks. The team runs 20 **on-demand** instances as a guaranteed baseline, and lets an autoscaler add up to 80 **spot** instances, spread across four instance types, for the burst.

If a chunk of spot capacity is reclaimed mid-burst, the baseline keeps processing uninterrupted while the autoscaler requests replacement spot capacity — cost drops sharply versus running the full 100 on-demand, with no loss of the guaranteed floor.

slides.subTitle: Autoscaling on a laggy metric
slides.markdown:
The wrong belief: any autoscaling metric works as long as a threshold is set. In practice, a metric with a long collection or aggregation delay — say, a 5-minute-averaged CPU metric — means the autoscaler is always reacting to load that already happened minutes ago.

The correct model: pick a metric that leads the actual bottleneck, with the shortest practical lag, and add a scale-up buffer earlier than feels necessary. A scale-up decision made on stale data arrives after the spike has already caused damage.
